theme: Do not fret; trust in the LORD, providence over the wicked
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 37:1-22 slowly, twice. This is a wisdom psalm, a long meditation on the apparent prosperity of the wicked and the patient confidence of the righteous. It is the perfect psalm for those who have been reading about Joseph’s unjust suffering.
settingTheScene: Psalm 37 is one of the great wisdom psalms, long, calm, deliberate. It addresses the question that has haunted believers in every generation: why do the wicked seem to prosper while the righteous suffer? David’s answer is patience and trust. Do not fret. Do not envy. The wicked will fade like grass; the righteous will inherit the land. The psalm fits Joseph’s situation exactly, he has just been imprisoned for refusing to sin, while the wicked seem to triumph.
observation: The psalm opens with three commands: “Fret not… be not envious… Trust in the LORD.”
The wicked are compared to grass that quickly fades.
Verse 4: “Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart.”
Verse 5: “Commit your way to the LORD; trust in him.” The verb “commit” literally means “roll”, roll your way onto him.
Verse 7: “Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him.” Stillness and waiting are part of righteousness.
Verse 11 anticipates Jesus’ Beatitude: “The meek shall inherit the land.”
The contrast continues: the wicked plot and gnash their teeth, but the LORD laughs because he sees their day coming.
Verse 18: “The LORD knows the days of the blameless, and their heritage will remain forever.”
interpretation:
Psalm 37 is one of the wisest psalms in the Psalter. It does not deny that the wicked prosper. It does not pretend life is fair. It accepts the painful reality and then offers the corrective: a long view. The wicked seem to flourish for a moment; the righteous inherit forever.

Three commands open the psalm. Fret not. Envy not. Trust. These are the daily disciplines of the believer facing apparent injustice. Fretting is the spiritual equivalent of constantly checking a wound. Envying the wicked is letting their apparent success poison your contentment. Trust is the alternative, letting God hold what you cannot control.

The reason for not fretting is the long view: the wicked are like grass. They look prosperous in the morning. By evening, they wither. Compared with eternity, the success of the wicked is brief. The temptation is to compare time spans incorrectly, to weigh ten years of someone’s worldly success against eternity and conclude that they are winning. But the comparison is wrong. They will fade. The righteous endure.

Verse 4 is one of the most quoted in the Psalter: “Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart.” This is sometimes misread as a transaction, delight in God and you will get what you want. But the deeper meaning is transformative: delight in the LORD, and your desires themselves will be reshaped. What you want will become what he wants. The desires of your heart, properly aligned with God, will indeed be granted, because they will be the right desires.

The image of “rolling your way onto the LORD” in verse 5 is wonderful. You roll your burden onto someone else, and you are free of it. The Christian life involves daily rolling, daily handing over to God what you cannot carry yourself.

Verse 11 anticipates Jesus’ Beatitude: “The meek shall inherit the land.” Jesus quoted this exact verse in Matthew 5:5. The meek, those who do not assert their rights, who do not fret about injustice, who do not envy the wicked, they get the inheritance in the end. The world thinks meekness is weakness. The Bible says meekness is the strongest posture, because it trusts the One who holds the future.

And the psalm gives us a striking image of God: “The LORD laughs at the wicked, for he sees that his day is coming.” God is not anxious about injustice. He laughs. Not in cruelty, but in confidence. He knows the end. He knows when the wicked will fall. He knows when his people will be vindicated. We can rest in that knowledge.
connection: Joseph has just been thrown into prison for refusing to sin. His brothers, who sold him into slavery, are eating well at home. Potiphar’s wife, who lied about him, sleeps in her bed. Joseph sleeps in chains. Psalm 37 is the song Joseph could have prayed. Do not fret. Trust the LORD. The wicked are like grass. The meek inherit. This is the wisdom that sustained Joseph in his unjust suffering, and it is the wisdom that sustains believers still.
application: Today, examine where you are fretting. What injustice in your life are you turning over and over? What success of someone else are you watching with envy? Bring it before God. Then practice the three commands: Fret not. Envy not. Trust. And practice the discipline of verse 4, delight yourself in the LORD. Not as a strategy to get what you want, but as a means of becoming someone whose wants are right.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what makes you fret or envy, and lay it before him.
Ask him to reshape your desires by delight in him.
Pray for patience to wait for him and not for your own way.
